title: Shipwreck (Acts 27–28:10)
hookLine: a storm, a wreck, everyone saved, and a viper on Malta

lines: WE SET SAIL: THE NARRATOR WAS ON BOARD.
cards: Acts 27 reads like a sea novel, told in the first person plural: we set sail, we were driven, we were cast ashore. The narrator was on board. Paul is a prisoner bound for Rome under a centurion named Julius.

It's late in the sailing season, and Paul warns them this voyage will bring damage and loss. The ship's master and owner want to push on to a better harbor, and the centurion listens to them, not to the prisoner.
A gentle south wind blows. They set out. Then a violent northeaster comes down off the island of Crete.

teach.h: NO SUN, NO STARS, NO HOPE.
teach.b: The ship can't face the wind, so they let it drive them. They throw cargo overboard, then the ship's tackle. For many days neither sun nor stars appear, and all hope of being saved, the text says, was taken away.
Then Paul stands up among them.
Be of good cheer, he says; an angel of God stood by me tonight: not one life will be lost, only the ship.
On the fourteenth night, near land, Paul urges everyone to eat, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "for there shall not an hair of the head of any of you perish."

He takes bread, gives thanks to God in front of them all, breaks it, and begins to eat. And everyone eats: two hundred seventy-six people, Luke counts. At daylight they run the ship aground and it breaks apart.

The soldiers plan to kill the prisoners so none escape, but the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stops them. Swimmers swim, the rest float on planks, and, the text says, they all got safe to land. The island is Malta.
The islanders show them unusual kindness and light a fire in the rain. Paul gathers a bundle of sticks, and a viper comes out from the heat and fastens on his hand.
A murderer, the islanders say; justice won't let him live. Paul shakes it into the fire and nothing happens.

teach.h: THEY ALL GOT SAFE TO LAND.
teach.b: They wait for him to swell up. When he doesn't, they change their minds and say he's a god. Luke tells it with a straight face.
Malta still keeps the feast of Saint Paul's Shipwreck every February tenth.

how: In Malta, the feast of Saint Paul's Shipwreck on February 10 is a public holiday with Mass and a procession, and Catholics there honor Paul as the island's father in faith.

games.q: you're Paul. fourteen days of storm, no one has eaten, everyone is terrified. what do you do?
o: urge everyone to eat, give thanks, break bread and eat first.
help the sailors lower the lifeboat.
games.why: he promises not a hair will be lost, takes bread, gives thanks before them all, breaks it and eats. they all take heart and eat.

practice: Think of a place where people around you are anxious: a family worry, a shaky job, a friend in a storm.
Paul didn't pretend the storm was small; he ate, gave thanks, and helped others eat, so picture yourself as the steady one in that room, with a slow breath, a plain kind word, maybe a meal.
If you pray, pray for the people in your boat.
